Would my running shoe burn in a Moon rov.answer: The running shoe is represented by a stand-in material, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass), not the shoe itself. In the NASA data used, there is no matching test of this material in the rover's air (34% oxygen at 0.56 atm), so it was not tested in this air — and not tested is not the same as safe.
Would my running shoe burn in a Moon rov.more: In a cabin fire, the shoe's fabric upper and laces would be the parts most likely to catch and spread flame, while foam and rubber can melt and add smoke. Flames behave differently without gravity: buoyancy-driven flow disappears, so oxygen reaches the flame mainly by slow diffusion and ventilation-driven flow, which can change how fast fire spreads. Higher oxygen concentrations make materials easier to ignite and burn faster, which is why the exact cabin air matters when judging fire risk.

Would my cotton shirt burn on the Statio.answer: The cotton shirt is represented by a stand-in material, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass), which was burned in tests on the Space Station. That material was tested in air like this cabin's (about 1 atm, with oxygen levels from 16.4% to 22.1%), so there is a matching test in this air in the NASA data used.
Would my cotton shirt burn on the Statio.more: In a cabin fire, clothing and other thin fabrics are often what first catches flame, so how they burn matters for escape time and smoke. In microgravity there is no buoyancy to carry hot gases away, so flames spread differently than on Earth and can creep along a surface in ways gravity would not allow. Higher oxygen concentrations make materials easier to ignite and burn faster, which is why the oxygen level in the surrounding air is tracked alongside each test.

Would a candle burn on Mars?.answer: The candle is a stand-in for the object, and the material card describes candle wax. In the NASA data used here, there is no matching test of this material in this air (34% oxygen at 0.56 atm), so not tested is not the same as safe. The closest recorded fire was BASS-II test F4 at 17.4% oxygen.
Would a candle burn on Mars?.more: In a cabin fire, small items like a candle's wax and wick matter because they can be the first things to ignite and spread flame to nearby materials. Flames behave differently without gravity: buoyancy-driven flow is absent, so ventilation and oxygen supply shape how a flame spreads. Higher oxygen concentrations make combustion easier and faster, which is why the exact air mixture matters when judging fire risk.

Will an NVIDIA H100 GPU burn on Mars?.more: Plastic parts like cases, windows and housings matter in a cabin fire because they can ignite, spread flame along surfaces, and give off smoke and fumes.
